## Territory and military

**Military.**

- Armies on land, fleets at sea; one fighting unit per province, bands and pirate ships among them. Caravans and couriers are travellers, not fighting units: they pass under the rules of travel ("Interception on the road").
- Diplomacy-style resolution, including convoys: strength is one plus supports, and ties bounce. No dice in combat.
- Supports can be given to any power, so a promised support is a checkable promise.
- **Battles: one season, losses, no dice** (decided 26 October 2026; built with army size in build order item 13). A season is a third of a year: room for a campaign and its one decisive battle, so a battle is decided within the season it is fought, and armies never stand and fight for months; only sieges last longer. An army's strength becomes its size, shaped by its commander's skill and the ground, plus the size of its supports, and the stronger side wins as now. The loser falls back to a neighbouring province its side holds or that stands empty, losing men in proportion to the margin it lost by; the winner loses men too, fewer. An army with nowhere to fall back, or beaten by far, is destroyed or scattered. Where it falls back is its commander's choice within his mandate ("retreat if outnumbered", "Command at a distance"), so the enemy cannot be sure of it. There are still no dice: a battle is uncertain because of what a king does not know, the enemy's numbers, its commander's skill and its orders, so every result has a cause the record can show ("Every error has a motive"). Until item 13 a dislodged army is destroyed, as now.

**Tempo of war.** Pillar 8 takes the game beyond Diplomacy's combat model. Early bot games showed why: Hatti could swallow Arzawa before any letter arrived, so diplomacy never got a chance.

- **Sieges (the priority).** Walled cities, and capitals above all, take several seasons to take. The besieger must keep the army in place and pay for it, while the besieged can still send envoys, beg for help and bargain. The vassal letters are full of sieges that dragged on while their rulers pleaded with the pharaoh; that window is where diplomacy happens. Getting a message out depends on the envoy's competence and courage and on how tight the siege is; the besieger may capture the envoy and read the tablets. Several messages need several envoys, or one envoy visiting courts in turn.
- **Campaign seasons (decided 21 October 2026: they arise from cost, without a rule; "Winter in the field" under "Seasons").** Bronze Age armies fought mainly in certain seasons; fewer war seasons a year slows everything naturally.
- **Distance-based marching (decided 19 October 2026; built with command at a distance, build order item 13).** Long marches take several seasons. How long military matters take is not fixed in advance (decided 19 October 2026): marches, levies and sieges start from the pace of letters, an envoy taking one or two seasons between capitals, and from what is realistic for the period, and balance tests then set them.
- **Slow absorption (decided; built with sieges, build order item 5).** Conquered land yields little at first, so rapid expansion pays less; from item 17 it may also revolt ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice").

**Walls and terrain (decided direction, built with sieges in item 5).** Defense comes from two separate sources:

- **Walls, the built defense.** They vary from place to place (Hattusa's massive walls on a rocky ridge, a Levantine village with none) and can be strengthened for gold and upkeep, a real choice between defense and expansion. With sieges, walls mainly set how long a city holds out, not only how many armies it takes to storm it.
- **Terrain, the natural defense.** Mountains and hills make a province harder to take. Terrain along a route matters as much: crossing a river such as the Euphrates or forcing a pass such as the Cilician Gates between Anatolia and Syria is harder than attacking across open ground, so these belong on the connection between two provinces. Deserts such as Sinai cost an army supplies rather than adding defense, except that an army in its own land pays no desert cost ("Different data, same rules"): Egypt's armies cross Sinai free because Egypt holds it, and so does anyone who takes it. Islands such as Alashiya are protected by the sea: today a landing counts as a crossing, and from item 7a a blockade decides ("Finer seas").
- **Simple whole numbers** keep resolution deterministic.

This also helps the smaller kings: Arzawa's mountains and Alashiya's sea become real advantages. The risk is tipping from too fast to stalemate if defense rises everywhere at once, which is why walls, terrain and sieges are tuned as one.

Longer wars mean longer games; sleeping seats are what make those affordable, since model calls scale with events, not with time.

**A kingdom falls with its capital** (decided 19 October 2026). When a power's capital is taken, the king has fallen and the kingdom with him: its remaining land passes to the conqueror, the power whose troops took the capital, and its debts die with it, as back pay already does. Before item 5 a kingdom fell only when it held no land, so a king who lost his capital fought on from his last provinces; this replaced that. Under slow absorption the land becomes the conqueror's over time rather than at once, so a conqueror gains an empire to hold, not a lump of score. A fallen kingdom's armies in the field are their commanders' to decide: once armies have commanders ("Generals lead armies" and "No commander, no mandate"), each commander chooses for himself whether to serve the conqueror, offer his army to another court, take land of his own, a new Idrimi, or turn outlaw with it. An army with nobody to command it may raise a captain from its own ranks, who faces the same choice, or else disbands ("A head rises where men lack one"); until commanders are built, all of them disband. An army no kingdom pays for is paid by the character who keeps it: its upkeep comes from his purse, his hoard, plunder or a loan, and troops he cannot pay desert, as a king's do. What he can afford is part of his decision, so a poor commander is pushed towards the conqueror or another court, and a rich one can afford to strike out alone. Once "the capital is wherever the king is" is built, a king who has moved his court is not taken with his old seat: the city that falls is no longer his capital, and he rules on from wherever he is. The other choices for the land, free cities or whoever reaches them first, characters included, were set aside for now. The siege package aimed for capitals to fall in most games, at about 5–10 seasons from the first hostile entry to a capital's fall; item 5 found them falling in about half the games, a median 9 to 10 seasons after the first entry, and whether that is what we want is judged in the balance pass (item 18), once game length is set.

**A fallen player's game is over** (decided 19 October 2026). As in Diplomacy, elimination is real; a fallen king does not return as a character. The player may watch the rest of the game in god view, as is standard, seeing everything but the drawn last season ("Random ending"): who lied to him, which envoy betrayed him, what the tablets really said. It is a setting, on by default, so a table of human players worried that a fallen player might pass hidden facts to a friend still in the game can turn it off; he then watches with what his kingdom knew when it fell until the game ends. Spectating an AI-only game keeps both god view and each king's own view, as now.

**How cities become free** (decided 20 October 2026), from systems already decided: conquered land not yet absorbed may revolt and break free, when the conditions below say so ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"); a governor who turns with the levies he raised, or a commander who keeps his army, may rule a city of his own (the new Idrimi); and a vassal that stops paying is free in practice unless its overlord comes to punish it. A fallen kingdom's land passes to the conqueror as newly conquered land, so it can revolt like any other. Land that breaks free with nobody at its head raises a ruler from its own people ("A head rises where men lack one", decided 21 October 2026).

**Revolt follows conditions, not dice** (decided 20 October 2026). Every province a power holds but has not fully absorbed carries an unrest level, summed from conditions the engine can see, and it revolts when unrest passes a threshold; the seeded dice only settle ties at the margin. What raises unrest:

- **How new the conquest is:** highest when just taken, falling as the land is absorbed;
- **hardship:** famine or another catastrophe there, levies raised from it, gold taken from it;
- **the master's weakness:** his armies beaten, his capital besieged, his troops busy elsewhere;
- **distance:** far from the king, by the measure of item 7;
- **a cause to rally to:** the province's old ruler alive and free, or a character of standing there who wants it;
- **outside help:** a rival's gold or envoys stirring it up, which is deniable like any bribe.

What lowers it: troops in or next to the province, a loyal governor there, policing (item 15), time, and a good harvest. A province that revolts becomes a free power of its own, under its old ruler or the character who led it, with the levies it can raise; troops of the master in the province fight them as combat says. The owner does not see the number: he learns of unrest as he learns of anything, from his governor (who may misreport it), his spies and travellers. First guesses for every weight and the threshold, tuned in build order item 18.

**What is absent on purpose.** No war declarations, no truces, no alliance flags, no opinion meters. A power at peace is simply one nobody is attacking.
